Sustaining Growth: Nurturing Motivation and Wellbeing
So, you’ve made it through the admissions process—maybe you’re even breathing a little easier now. It’s tempting to let those good habits slide, right? But here’s the thing: the very qualities that got you or your child into a top school are the same ones that’ll keep fueling growth and happiness down the road. Motivation, curiosity, emotional health... these aren’t boxes you check just once. They’re lifelong companions on the journey.
Motivation, especially for young people, can be a bit of a balancing act. It really blossoms in places where effort gets noticed, interests are encouraged, and setbacks aren’t something to fear—they’re just part of how we learn. So, how can families help keep that spark alive?
First, celebrate progress. Don’t just wait for the big finish line—cheer on the small wins and those tiny steps forward. Next, encourage autonomy. Let kids make choices about their learning and activities. That sense of ownership goes a long way. And don’t forget about balance. Mixing schoolwork with hobbies, downtime, and social moments helps protect against burnout. Finally, model lifelong learning. Show that curiosity isn’t just for the classroom—it’s a family value.
Think about a student who’s worked hard for entrance exams. Once it’s over, it’s normal to feel a bit deflated. Instead of letting that momentum fade, why not channel it into something new? Maybe it’s exploring a creative project, joining a club, or giving back through volunteering. Shifting the focus to fresh goals can really help keep things moving in a positive direction.
And let’s not forget wellbeing. The drive for achievement can sometimes stir up anxiety or self-doubt. That’s why open communication is so important. Regular check-ins, a willingness to reach out for support, and simple routines—like sharing meals or taking walks together—create those moments for connection and reflection.
When you look at the bigger picture, all those habits and mindsets built during the admissions journey? They’re not just for getting into school. They’re real tools for life—helping young people navigate new chapters, face challenges head-on, and find meaning in what they do, no matter what the outcome looks like.
